summary.text: Couple the two evolutions by viewing the larger one as the smaller configuration plus a single extra chip; gaplessness and mass conservation force the smaller system’s penultimate state to be \([1,\ldots,1,2]\), while frontier and leading-run invariants place that chip one or two sites short of the new endpoint when the smaller system settles. Thereafter the smaller configuration is fixed and the chip advances one site per step through its unit cells, so the larger system settles exactly one or two steps later.

full_proof.text:
Let configurations be indexed by the nonnegative integers. We extend every finite configuration by zeros to the right. For a function
\[
M:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,
\]
define one automaton step \(F\) by
\[
(FM)(0)=\left\lceil\frac{M(0)}2\right\rceil
       =\frac{M(0)+1}{2},
\]
and, for \(i\geq 0\),
\[
(FM)(i+1)=\left\lceil\frac{M(i+1)}2\right\rceil
             +\left\lfloor\frac{M(i)}2\right\rfloor
 =\frac{M(i+1)+1}{2}+\frac{M(i)}2,
\]
where the displayed integer quotients are rounded down. Thus a cell retains the ceiling of half its mass and receives the floor of half the mass of its left neighbor.

For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(M_n^t\) denote the configuration after \(t\) steps from mass \(n\) concentrated at the origin:
\[
M_n^0(i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
\qquad M_n^{t+1}=F(M_n^t).
\]
Let
\[
T_n(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<n,\\0,&i\geq n.\end{cases}
\]
This is the desired stable configuration. Direct substitution in the definition of \(F\) shows that
\[
F(T_n)=T_n. \tag{1}
\]
We will first prove the result for these zero-extended functional configurations, and at the end identify their settling time with the sequence \(a(n)\) defined using finite lists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Basic structure of the evolving configurations
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The support of \(M_n^t\) is contained in \(\{0,1,\ldots,t\}\). Indeed, this is clear at time zero, and in one step mass can move at most one place to the right. More explicitly, if \(M(i)=0\) for every \(i\geq N\), then \((FM)(i)=0\) for every \(i\geq N+1\).

We also need that the support has no gaps. Call \(M\) gapless if
\[
M(i)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M(i+1)=0
\]
for every \(i\). The initial configuration is gapless. If \(M\) is gapless and \((FM)(i)=0\), then both nonnegative terms contributing to \((FM)(i)\) vanish. At \(i=0\), this forces \(M(0)=0\), hence \(M(1)=0\), and therefore \((FM)(1)=0\). At \(i=k+1\), vanishing of \((FM)(k+1)\) forces \(M(k+1)=0\); gaplessness gives \(M(k+2)=0\), and consequently \((FM)(k+2)=0\). Thus \(FM\) is gapless. By induction every \(M_n^t\) is gapless. In particular, once one entry is zero, all entries to its right are zero.

Total mass is conserved. To see this, take \(N\) with \(M(N)=0\) and with the support of \(M\) contained below \(N\). Summing the next configuration through position \(N\), every old cell contributes once through its retained part and once through the part it sends right. Hence
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{N}(FM)(i)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\left(
   \left\lceil\frac{M(i)}2\right\rceil+
   \left\lfloor\frac{M(i)}2\right\rfloor\right)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}M(i). \tag{2}
\]
It follows that every \(M_n^t\) has total mass \(n\).

Gaplessness and mass conservation imply the useful containment property
\[
M_n^t(i)=0\qquad(i\geq n). \tag{3}
\]
For if \(M_n^t(i)>0\) for some \(i\geq n\), gaplessness implies that every entry at positions \(0,1,\ldots,i\) is nonzero and hence at least \(1\). The total mass would then be at least \(i+1\geq n+1\), contradicting mass conservation.

We will use two boundary parameters. For a configuration that is eventually zero, let
\[
\ell(M)=\min\{i:M(i)\ne1\}
\]
be the length of its initial run of ones, and let
\[
r(M)=\min\{i:M(i)=0\}
\]
be its occupied frontier. Thus \(M(i)=1\) for \(i<\ell(M)\), and, for a gapless configuration, \(M(i)=0\) for all \(i\geq r(M)\).

The target has
\[
\ell(T_n)=n. \tag{4}
\]
Also, \(T_m=T_n\) implies \(m=n\), since if, say, \(m<n\), the two functions differ at position \(m\).

Before continuing, we establish that the system really does reach its target. Define the first moment
\[
P_n(t)=\sum_i iM_n^t(i),
\]
where the sum is finite. In one step, every unit of mass sent from position \(i\) to position \(i+1\) raises the moment by one. Therefore
\[
P_n(t+1)=P_n(t)+\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{M_n^t(i)}2\right\rfloor. \tag{5}
\]
If all entries of \(M_n^t\) are at most \(1\), then (3), together with total mass \(n\), forces all of positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\) to contain \(1\); hence \(M_n^t=T_n\). Consequently, while the state is not the target, some entry is at least \(2\), and the sum on the right of (5) is at least \(1\). Thus the moment increases by at least one at every unsettled step.

On the other hand, by (3), every nonzero mass lies at a position less than \(n\), so the coarse bound
\[
P_n(t)\leq n\sum_iM_n^t(i)=n^2 \tag{6}
\]
holds. If the system never settled, (5) would give \(P_n(t)\geq t\), contradicting (6) for \(t>n^2\). Therefore the settling time
\[
\tau_n=\min\{t:M_n^t=T_n\} \tag{7}
\]
is well-defined. By (1), the state remains equal to \(T_n\) at every time after \(\tau_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Coupling the systems of masses \(n\) and \(n+1\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(e_p\) denote the configuration consisting of one unit at position \(p\) and zero elsewhere. The key elementary identity is
\[
F(M+e_p)=FM+e_{p'}, \tag{8}
\]
where
\[
p'=\begin{cases}
p+1,&M(p)\text{ is odd},\\
p,&M(p)\text{ is even}.
\end{cases} \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, adding one to \(M(p)\) affects only the retained contribution at \(p\) and the sent contribution arriving at \(p+1\). If \(M(p)\) is even, its ceiling half increases by one and its floor half does not, so the extra unit remains at \(p\). If \(M(p)\) is odd, its ceiling half does not increase and its floor half does, so the extra unit appears at \(p+1\). All other coordinates are unchanged. This also covers \(p=0\), where there is no incoming contribution from the left.

Define the chip position \(q_t=q_t(n)\) recursively by
\[
q_0=0,
\qquad
q_{t+1}=\begin{cases}
q_t+1,&M_n^t(q_t)\text{ is odd},\\
q_t,&M_n^t(q_t)\text{ is even}.
\end{cases} \tag{10}
\]
Since \(M_{n+1}^0=M_n^0+e_0\), repeated use of (8) gives the coupling identity
\[
M_{n+1}^t=M_n^t+e_{q_t} \qquad\text{for every }t. \tag{11}
\]
Thus the entire difference between the two systems is a single chip which either remains in place or advances by one at each step.

The chip never passes the occupied frontier of the \(n\)-system:
\[
q_t\leq r(M_n^t). \tag{12}
\]
First note that the frontier cannot move left under \(F\). If \(i<r(M)\), then \(M(i)>0\), and the ceiling contribution from \(M(i)\) to \((FM)(i)\) is positive. Hence \((FM)(i)>0\), so
\[
r(FM)\geq r(M). \tag{13}
\]
Now (12) follows by induction. It is clear at time zero. If the chip stays put, use (13). If it advances, then \(M_n^t(q_t)\) is odd and therefore nonzero. Since the state is gapless and \(q_t\leq r(M_n^t)\), this rules out equality with the frontier; thus \(q_t<r(M_n^t)\), and
\[
q_{t+1}=q_t+1\leq r(M_n^t)\leq r(M_n^{t+1}).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The leading run of ones
--------------------------------------------------------------------

If \(i<\ell(M)\), then \(M(i)=1\). It follows immediately from the update rule that
\[
(FM)(i)=1\qquad(i<\ell(M)). \tag{14}
\]
At the first non-one position itself, the left neighbor, when present, is \(1\), whose sent half is zero. Hence
\[
(FM)(\ell(M))=\left\lceil\frac{M(\ell(M))}{2}\right\rceil. \tag{15}
\]

Suppose that the leading run grows by at least two in one step:
\[
\ell(FM)\geq\ell(M)+2. \tag{16}
\]
Write \(s=\ell(M)\), and assume, as is true for all our finite-support states, that \(M(s)\ne1\). Since positions \(s\) and \(s+1\) of \(FM\) are both \(1\), equation (15) gives
\[
\left\lceil\frac{M(s)}2\right\rceil=1.
\]
The possibilities are \(M(s)=1\) or \(2\), and the first is excluded by the definition of \(s\). Thus
\[
M(s)=2. \tag{17}
\]
At the next position,
\[
1=(FM)(s+1)=\left\lceil\frac{M(s+1)}2\right\rceil+
                \left\lfloor\frac{2}{2}\right\rfloor,
\]
so
\[
M(s+1)=0. \tag{18}
\]
If \(M\) is gapless, (18) makes every later entry zero. Together with the initial \(s\) ones and (17), a direct application of \(F\) then gives
\[
FM=T_{s+2}. \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, positions below \(s\) remain \(1\), position \(s\) receives the retained half of \(2\), position \(s+1\) receives the sent half of \(2\), and every later position is zero.

Applied to an evolving mass-\(n\) state, this shows:
\[
M_n^{t+1}\ne T_n
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\ell(M_n^{t+1})\leq\ell(M_n^t)+1. \tag{20}
\]
For otherwise (16)--(19) would show that \(M_n^{t+1}=T_{s+2}\). A state of total mass \(n\) which equals a target \(T_m\) must have \(m=n\), because \(T_m\) has total mass \(m\). Hence that next state would be \(T_n\), contrary to the assumption.

We can now relate the chip to the leading run. While the \(n\)-system is unsettled,
\[
\ell(M_n^t)\leq q_t+1. \tag{21}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time zero, position \(1\) is zero, so \(\ell(M_n^0)\leq1=q_0+1\). For the induction step, if \(M_n^{t+1}\ne T_n\), then also \(M_n^t\ne T_n\), because the target is fixed by \(F\). Thus the induction hypothesis applies. Moreover,
\[
\ell(M_n^t)\leq q_{t+1}. \tag{22}
\]
To see this, if \(q_t<\ell(M_n^t)\), then \(M_n^t(q_t)=1\), which is odd, so the chip advances and
\(q_{t+1}=q_t+1\); combining this with the induction hypothesis
\(\ell(M_n^t)\leq q_t+1\) gives (22). If instead \(q_t\geq\ell(M_n^t)\), the chip never moves left, so again (22) holds. Finally (20) and (22) yield
\[
\ell(M_n^{t+1})\leq\ell(M_n^t)+1\leq q_{t+1}+1,
\]
which proves (21).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The state immediately before settling
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Assume \(n\geq2\), and suppose
\[
M_n^t\ne T_n,
\qquad
M_n^{t+1}=T_n. \tag{23}
\]
We claim that, writing \(s=\ell(M_n^t)\),
\[
s=n-2,
\qquad M_n^t(n-2)=2,
\qquad M_n^t(i)=0\quad(i\geq n-1). \tag{24}
\]

Since \(F(M_n^t)=T_n\), its leading run has length \(n\). First, \(s\leq n\): if \(s>n\), (14) would give \((FM_n^t)(n)=1\), whereas \(T_n(n)=0\). We cannot have \(s=n\), because then \(M_n^t\) is \(1\) at every position below \(n\), and by containment (3) is zero from \(n\) onward; it would already equal \(T_n\), contrary to (23).

Nor can \(s=n-1\). In that case \((FM_n^t)(n-1)=1\), and (15), together with \(M_n^t(s)\ne1\), forces \(M_n^t(n-1)=2\). But then the sent half of this \(2\) makes \((FM_n^t)(n)\geq1\), contradicting \(T_n(n)=0\). Therefore
\[
s\leq n-2.
\]
Since \(\ell(FM_n^t)=n\), the leading run has grown by at least two. Equations (17)--(19) now apply and show
\[
FM_n^t=T_{s+2}.
\]
But it also equals \(T_n\), and targets of different sizes are distinct. Hence \(s+2=n\). Equations (17), (18), and gaplessness give exactly (24).

We can now locate the chip at the settling time. For every \(n\geq1\),
\[
q_{\tau_n}<n,
\qquad
n\leq q_{\tau_n}+2. \tag{25}
\]
For \(n=1\), the initial state is already \(T_1\), so \(\tau_1=0\) and \(q_{\tau_1}=0\), proving (25).

Now let \(n=m+2\). Since \(n\geq2\), \(\tau_n\geq1\); write \(\tau_n=t+1\). By minimality of \(\tau_n\), conditions (23) hold. The penultimate description (24) says
\[
\ell(M_n^t)=m,
\quad M_n^t(m)=2,
\quad M_n^t(i)=0\ (i\geq m+1).
\]
The first zero is therefore exactly at \(m+1\): entries below \(m\) are \(1\), the entry at \(m\) is \(2\), and the entry at \(m+1\) is zero. Thus (12) gives
\[
q_t\leq m+1,
\]
while (21) gives
\[
m\leq q_t+1.
\]
There are three relevant cases for the last chip update.

* If \(q_t<m\), then the chip lies in the leading run of ones, so it advances by one. The two bounds force \(q_t\geq m-1\), hence \(q_{t+1}=m\).
* If \(q_t=m\), the chip sees mass \(2\), which is even, so it stays at \(m\).
* If \(q_t>m\), the upper bound forces \(q_t=m+1\); it sees mass \(0\), so it stays at \(m+1\).

Thus
\[
q_{\tau_n}=q_{t+1}\in\{m,m+1\}=
\{n-2,n-1\},
\]
which is precisely (25).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Exact recurrence for the settling times
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(n\geq1\), put
\[
q=q_{\tau_n},
\qquad d=n-q.
\]
By (25),
\[
d\in\{1,2\}. \tag{26}
\]
We will prove the stronger exact formula
\[
\tau_{n+1}=\tau_n+d
 =\tau_n+n-q_{\tau_n}. \tag{27}
\]

After time \(\tau_n\), the \(n\)-system remains at \(T_n\). In this target, every position below \(n\) contains the odd value \(1\), while position \(n\) contains the even value \(0\). Consequently, after \(k\) further steps, the chip position is
\[
q_{\tau_n+k}=\min(q+k,n). \tag{28}
\]
This follows immediately by induction: while the chip is below \(n\), it sees a \(1\) and advances; once at \(n\), it sees a \(0\) and remains there.

At \(k=d=n-q\), equation (28) gives \(q_{\tau_n+d}=n\). Using the coupling (11), stability of the \(n\)-system, and the identity
\[
T_{n+1}=T_n+e_n,
\]
we obtain
\[
M_{n+1}^{\tau_n+d}
 =M_n^{\tau_n+d}+e_{q_{\tau_n+d}}
 =T_n+e_n=T_{n+1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\tau_{n+1}\leq\tau_n+d. \tag{29}
\]

It remains to prove that no earlier time works. Suppose for contradiction that for some
\(t<\tau_n+d\),
\[
M_{n+1}^t=T_{n+1}.
\]
By the coupling and \(T_{n+1}=T_n+e_n\),
\[
M_n^t+e_{q_t}=T_n+e_n. \tag{30}
\]
Evaluate (30) at position \(n\). By containment (3), \(M_n^t(n)=0\), and also \(T_n(n)=0\). Therefore the chip contribution at position \(n\) must be \(1\), which forces
\[
q_t=n. \tag{31}
\]
If \(t<\tau_n\), then substituting (31) into (30) and cancelling the same unit configuration \(e_n\) from both sides gives \(M_n^t=T_n\), contradicting the minimality of \(\tau_n\). Thus \(t\geq\tau_n\), so write \(t=\tau_n+k\). Equation (28), together with (31), implies \(q+k\geq n\), or \(k\geq n-q=d\). Hence
\[
t=\tau_n+k\geq\tau_n+d,
\]
again contradicting the assumed strict inequality. This proves the reverse inequality to (29), and hence the recurrence (27).

Combining (26) and (27), we have proved
\[
\tau_{n+1}=\tau_n+1
\quad\text{or}\quad
\tau_{n+1}=\tau_n+2
\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{32}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Identification with the list-defined sequence \(a(n)\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It remains only to justify that \(\tau_n\) is exactly the quantity \(a(n)\) in the statement. The original definition uses finite lists and, after applying the update, deletes trailing zeros. For a finite list \(L\), let \(\widehat L(i)\) be its \(i\)-th entry when \(i\) is within the list and \(0\) otherwise.

Deleting trailing zeros does not change \(\widehat L\). Before trimming, the list update forms the coordinatewise sum of
\[
\left(\left\lceil\frac{L(0)}2\right\rceil,
\left\lceil\frac{L(1)}2\right\rceil,\ldots,0\right)

after appending one final zero, and
\[
\left(0,
\left\lfloor\frac{L(0)}2\right\rfloor,
\left\lfloor\frac{L(1)}2\right\rfloor,\ldots\right).
\]
Therefore its zero extension is exactly \(F(\widehat L)\). Starting from the one-element list \([n]\), induction on time gives
\[
\widehat{L_n^t}=M_n^t, \tag{33}
\]
where \(L_n^t\) is the list configuration after \(t\) updates.

For \(n>0\), the initial list \([n]\) has no trailing zero, and every later list is explicitly trimmed, so none of these lists has a trailing zero. The target list consisting of \(n\) copies of \(1\) also has no trailing zero. Two finite lists with no trailing zero and with the same zero extension must be equal: their last nonzero positions determine the same length, and then equality of their zero extensions gives equality entry by entry. It follows from (33) that, for every \(n>0\) and every \(t\),
\[
L_n^t=[1,1,\ldots,1]\text{ (\(n\) entries)}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M_n^t=T_n. \tag{34}
\]
Thus the least list time in the definition of \(a(n)\) equals the least functional time in (7):
\[
a(n)=\tau_n\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{35}
\]
Finally, substituting (35) into (32) yields, for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
a(n+1)=a(n)+1
\quad\text{or}\quad
a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\},
\]
as required.
